Current: Federal rules (2024) cap initial terms at 3 months; many states restrict or ban these plans.
Proposed: A 2024 federal rule limits new plans to a 3-month initial term and 4 months total, but in August 2025 the Departments of Labor, HHS and Treasury said they will not prioritize enforcing it while they write a new rule; state law often sets the real limit, and many states restrict or ban these plans.
Reason: Outdated: the 2024 caps (3 months initial, 4 months total incl. renewals) are under a federal non-enforcement policy since 7 Aug 2025 and new rulemaking is pending, so stating the cap as the operative rule misleads.

Current: A tax-advantaged savings account for medical costs, available with a high-deductible health plan.
Proposed: A tax-advantaged savings account for medical costs, available if you have a qualifying high-deductible health plan (since 2026 this includes ACA bronze and catastrophic plans).
Reason: Outdated for 2026: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made bronze and catastrophic plans HSA-compatible from 1 Jan 2026 (IRS Notice 2026-5), plus direct primary care and telehealth safe harbors.

Proposed: IRS sets minimum deductibles and maximum out-of-pocket limits each year; since 2026, ACA bronze and catastrophic plans also count as HSA-compatible even if they don't meet the standard HDHP test.
Reason: Missing 2026 change that materially affects who can open an HSA.

Current: An employer account where you set aside pre-tax money for medical costs; unused money is usually lost at year-end.
Proposed: An employer account where you set aside pre-tax money for medical costs; money left at year-end is lost unless your plan offers a limited carryover or a grace period.
Reason: Misleading: plans may allow a carryover (up to $680 for 2026) or a 2.5-month grace period; 'usually lost' overstates forfeiture.

Proposed: The federal No Surprises Act (2022) bans balance billing for most emergency care and for certain out-of-network care at in-network hospitals and surgery centers.
Reason: Omission on a consumer site: the key federal protection against balance billing is missing, so the definition implies all out-of-network bills can be balance-billed.

Current: Coverage for auto businesses such as repair shops and dealers, including customers' cars in their care (garagekeepers).
Proposed: Liability coverage for auto businesses such as repair shops and dealers, for injuries and damage arising from their premises, operations and autos; damage to customers' cars in their care needs separate garagekeepers coverage.
Reason: Wrong: garage liability excludes property in the insured's care, custody or control, including customers' cars; garagekeepers is a separate coverage (Section III of the garage form).

Proposed: ISO's Auto Dealers Coverage Form (CA 00 25) has largely replaced the older Garage Coverage Form (CA 00 05) for dealers.
Reason: Useful current context; the term 'garage policy' now mainly survives for non-dealer garages.

Current: The Inflation Reduction Act capped Part D out-of-pocket costs starting 2025.
Proposed: The Inflation Reduction Act capped Part D out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000 in 2025, indexed each year ($2,100 in 2026).
Reason: Accurate but vague; adding the dollar cap and indexing makes it useful and current.

Current: The ACA sets a federal maximum each year for in-network essential health benefits.
Proposed: The ACA sets a federal maximum each year for in-network essential health benefits ($10,600 self-only / $21,200 family for 2026).
Reason: Add current figures; 2026 limit was revised upward by the June 2025 Marketplace Integrity rule.

Proposed: From plan year 2026, CMS extended the hardship exemption to people who can't get premium tax credits or cost-sharing reductions because of their income, widening access to catastrophic plans.
Reason: Definition is still correct, but eligibility widened materially in 2026.

Current: Each state runs its own program funded by employer taxes.
Proposed: Each state runs its own program, funded mainly by state and federal employer payroll taxes; workers also contribute in Alaska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
Reason: 'Funded by employer taxes' is incomplete: three states also collect employee contributions.

Current: NAIC Actuarial Guideline 49-A limits illustrated rates.
Proposed: NAIC Actuarial Guideline 49-A (2020), updated by AG 49-B (2023), limits illustrated rates and multiplier/volatility-controlled index features.
Reason: AG 49-A has been supplemented by AG 49-B (2023); citing only 49-A is slightly out of date.

Current: Considered an 'excepted benefit' under federal law.
Proposed: Treated as an 'excepted benefit' under federal law (exempt from ACA rules) when offered as independent, non-coordinated specified-disease coverage.
Reason: The excepted-benefit status is conditional, not automatic.

Current: The federal health insurance program for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities.
Proposed: The federal health insurance program for people 65 and older, some younger people with disabilities, and people with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or ALS.
Reason: Omits ESRD/ALS eligibility, a standard part of the Medicare definition.

Current: A tax-free swap of one life insurance or annuity policy for another under IRS Section 1035.
Proposed: A tax-free exchange under IRS Section 1035 of a life insurance, annuity or long-term care policy for a similar or allowed contract (e.g. life to annuity is allowed, annuity to life is not).
Reason: 'Swap for another' implies any direction; Section 1035 only permits certain exchanges.

Current: Federal workers' compensation for maritime workers such as dockworkers and ship repairers.
Proposed: Workers' compensation required by the federal Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act for maritime workers such as dockworkers and ship repairers, usually bought from private insurers.
Reason: 'Federal workers' compensation' can be confused with FECA (for federal employees); USL&H is a federally mandated coverage, not a federal program.

Current: A federal index-based program paying ranchers when rainfall in their area falls below normal.
Proposed: A federally subsidized crop insurance plan (USDA RMA, sold by private insurers) that pays ranchers when rainfall in their area's grid falls below normal.
Reason: Clarify it is a crop insurance plan sold by Approved Insurance Providers, not a direct government payment program.
Risk management is a core, frequently used term in US commercial insurance work (risk managers, RIMS, ARM designation); 'Low' understates it.
